attacks.claim: The public Recent signers panel renders full name and postal code for every confirmed signer, which violates the agreed rule that public signer lists show at most first name, last initial and city. Once live, this publishes personal data to anyone who loads a petition page, and scrapers and caches can keep copies after a rollback.
attacks.evidence:
{{ s.city }} {{ s.postal_code }} and
  • {{ s.full_name }} ...

attacks.claim: The Recent signers panel exposes EU signers' personal data publicly without a lawful basis or minimisation. This contradicts the stated GDPR commitment and the artifact's own claim that the panel shows signers 'without exposing signers'.
attacks.evidence: "Public 'Recent signers' panel ... showing first name + last initial and city, so visitors can see momentum without exposing signers." vs. template showing full_name and postal_code

attacks.claim: The newsletter opt-in is pre-ticked, which is not valid GDPR consent for EU signers. The artifact also says signers 'can choose' to receive updates, which contradicts the default.
attacks.evidence: <input type="checkbox" id="news" name="newsletter_opt_in" value="1" checked>

attacks.claim: Validation errors are conveyed only by a red border and background. The aria-live region is never populated, the fields get no aria-invalid or aria-describedby, and the error text is never written. Screen reader users receive no error message, which fails WCAG 2.1 AA 3.3.1 and the agreed AA requirement.
attacks.evidence: ... form.elements[name].classList.add('is-invalid'); (no text set, no aria-invalid)

attacks.claim: The client handles only 422 and 2xx responses. A 409 duplicate signature or a 5xx produces no visible message, so the user clicks Sign and nothing happens. The artifact's QA covers the 409 server response but not what the user sees.
attacks.evidence: if (res.status === 422) {...} if (res.ok) window.location = ...; (no branch for 409 or 5xx) vs. "Duplicate signature (same email) rejected with 409 | Pass"

attacks.claim: The WCAG 2.1 AA claim rests only on an automated axe-core scan with zero violations. Automated scans miss error identification and screen reader behaviour, and the template contradicts the claim (empty aria-live region). No manual or assistive technology testing is reported.
attacks.evidence: "axe-core automated scan on sign page | 0 violations" (no manual or screen reader testing listed)

attacks.claim: EU personal data may be stored in us-east-1 whenever the postal code does not resolve to an EU region, which is a default that is unsafe for EU residents. Postal code is also a weak residency signal. The DPA with Postmark does not by itself establish a transfer mechanism for the US storage.
attacks.evidence: Stored in ... eu-central-1 for EU-resolved postal codes, us-east-1 otherwise.

attacks.claim: No retention period is defined for confirmed signatures, and there is no described path for erasure requests or for withdrawing newsletter consent. Both are GDPR requirements for EU signers.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention for confirmed signer email and postal code; ABSENT: erasure or consent-withdrawal flow. Only the unconfirmed 7-day purge is stated.

attacks.claim: The sign form posts to a state-changing endpoint with no CSRF token shown. A third-party page could submit signatures on behalf of a victim where cookie protections are absent, which undermines petition integrity.
attacks.evidence: <form class="sign-form" action="/p/{{ petition.slug }}/sign" method="post" novalidate> (ABSENT: csrf token field or header)

attacks.claim: The success path reads a Location header from a fetch response that follows redirects by default, so the header may be absent and the navigation may target 'null'. QA reports the happy path passing, so this is a possible issue rather than a confirmed one.
attacks.evidence: const res = await fetch(form.action, { method: 'POST', body: new FormData(form) }); ... window.location = res.headers.get('Location');

attacks.claim: If the server returns a field name not present in the form, form.elements[name] is undefined and the handler throws. An empty fields array also makes fields[0] undefined.
attacks.evidence: for (const name of fields) form.elements[name].classList.add('is-invalid'); form.elements[fields[0]].focus();

attacks.claim: Load testing covers only signing writes at 400/s. The read path (recent_signers query on each page render, and 15s polling) is not load-tested for a viral petition, though the 10s CDN cache mitigates much of the risk.
attacks.evidence: "Load: 400 signatures/s sustained for 10 min, p95 210ms" (no read-path load test listed)

attacks.claim: The rollback plan does not say whether the Recent signers panel is behind the flag, whether already-published signer data is removed, or whether the 7-day purge continues after rollback.
attacks.evidence: "Rollback: flip petitions_signing off; sign form is replaced by ... 'Follow this petition' button." (ABSENT: panel flag and data removal)

attacks.claim: Confirmation depends on a single email vendor (Postmark) with no fallback, and alerting covers only bounce rate. A Postmark outage would silently leave signatures unconfirmed.
attacks.evidence: "Watch sign_submit_error_rate (< 0.5%) and confirmation email bounce rate (< 2%)" (ABSENT: send-failure alert, fallback provider)

attacks.claim: Single-provider dependency on Postmark for all confirmations, with no described exit path.
attacks.evidence: "Confirmation emails go through Postmark"

attacks.claim: Client validation and server validation are coupled through an undocumented 422 contract, which makes the flow harder to test independently.
attacks.evidence: const { fields } = await res.json(); (no contract documented)

attacks.claim: No gate-worthy issue found under this lens.
attacks.evidence: n/a

attacks.evidence: n/a

attacks.claim: Unconfirmed signatures may block re-signing with the same email, which could frustrate users who never received the confirmation email. The artifact does not say.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: re-sign behaviour for unconfirmed duplicate email

attacks.claim: The 10%/100% rollout is gated only on error and bounce rates, with no privacy or consent metric. Given the publication issue, the rollout would not catch the data exposure.
attacks.evidence: "Watch sign_submit_error_rate (< 0.5%) and confirmation email bounce rate (< 2%) for 24h."
